topic.angle: Each strand is a template for its partner

body.claim: When a cell copies its DNA, each old strand becomes the template for a new partner strand.
body.why: The double helix is unwound and separated, and each strand guides the building of a matching strand. Every new molecule keeps one original strand and gains one new one. DNA polymerases do the building and can remove a wrong piece, which is part of why copying is near-perfect.

probes.question: After DNA is copied, what does each new double helix contain?
options: One original strand and one newly made strand
A mix of short original and new fragments only

probes.question: True or false: DNA polymerases can remove a mismatched piece while copying, a step called proofreading.

claims.claim: Each old strand becomes the template for a new partner strand
claims.quote: each strand of the original DNA molecule then serves as a template for the production of a complementary counterpart strand

claims.claim: Every new molecule keeps one original strand and gains one new one (probe 1 answer)
claims.quote: each replicated DNA molecule is composed of one original DNA strand as well as one newly synthesized strand.

claims.claim: The helix is unwound and separated; each strand guides a matching strand
claims.quote: The double helix is 'unzipped' and unwound, then each separated strand (turquoise) acts as a template for replicating a new partner strand (green).
Most prominently, DNA polymerase synthesizes the new strands by incorporating nucleotides that complement the nucleotides of the template strand.

claims.claim: Polymerases can remove a wrong piece (proofreading), part of near-perfect copying (probe 2)
claims.quote: Some DNA polymerases can also delete nucleotides from the end of a developing strand in order to fix mismatched bases.
Cellular proofreading and error-checking mechanisms ensure near-perfect fidelity for DNA replication.
